conventions.convention: A response surface is a specified polynomial approximation on a declared region, with consistently coded coordinates; its definition asserts neither physical adequacy nor validity outside that region. The second-order form is m(x)=β₀+xᵀβ+xᵀBx with symmetric B.

Candidate sets are finite and nonempty, p≥1, approximate weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and M(ξ)=Σξₓf(x)f(x)ᵀ. Nonsingular means positive definite. D-, A-, E-, and c-optimality are defined among nonsingular designs.
Exact n-run designs have weights nₓ/n for nonnegative integer counts summing to n≥1. Their information matrices use the same normalized-weight convention as approximate designs.

A central composite design is a multiset union of its declared full or regular fractional factorial core, axial runs ±αeⱼ with α>0, and m₀≥1 center copies. Coincident runs retain multiplicity; estimability, rotatability, and orthogonal blocking are separate checks.

The quadratic stationary-point theorem assumes B is nonsingular and classifies the ambient polynomial. Its regional local classification requires x₀∈int(R); boundary or exterior points receive no constrained-optimum conclusion.

load_bearing.statement: An approximate design has weights ξₓ∈[0,1] summing to one and information matrix M(ξ)=Σξₓf(x)f(x)ᵀ. D-optimality maximizes log det M(ξ) among nonsingular designs; exact n-run designs have weights nₓ/n with nonnegative integer counts summing to n.
For p≥1 and real symmetric positive-definite A₀,A₁, log det((1−t)A₀+tA₁)≥(1−t)log det A₀+t log det A₁ for every t∈[0,1].

For a finite nonempty candidate set and a nonsingular approximate design ξ*, write M*=M(ξ*) and u*(x)=f(x)ᵀ(M*)⁻¹f(x). Then ξ* is D-optimal among nonsingular approximate designs if and only if u*(x)≤p for every candidate. Whenever this holds, u*(x)=p on supp(ξ*). No existence of a nonsingular optimum is asserted.
A second-order response-surface model on a declared region R⊆ℝᵏ, k≥1, has the form m(x)=β₀+xᵀβ+xᵀBx, where β₀∈ℝ, β∈ℝᵏ, and B is real symmetric.

For symmetric nonsingular B, the ambient quadratic polynomial has unique stationary point x₀=−½B⁻¹β. Positive eigenvalues give a strict minimum, negative eigenvalues a strict maximum, and both signs a saddle. The same local classification holds within R when x₀∈int(R); no constrained-optimum conclusion is supplied at boundary or exterior points.

published_dependencies.used_for: The real coordinate inner product and orthonormality of the standard basis in the quadratic classification and log-determinant proof.
The equivalence between real matrix symmetry and self-adjointness needed for spectral diagonalization.
Real eigenvalues and orthonormal diagonalization of symmetric matrices; curvature classification, positive inverse square roots, and the E-optimality definition.
Computing the determinant of the diagonal eigenvalue matrix in the log-determinant proof.
Passing from orthogonal diagonalization to the positive product-of-eigenvalues determinant.
The positive-size Leibniz determinant convention and det Iₚ=1.
The cofactor and adjugate interface supporting Jacobi's formula, including the locally defined determinant-one empty minor for size one.
The cofactor expansion underlying the cited determinant differential.
Reducing the adjugate determinant differential to the inverse-matrix Jacobi formula.
The matrix product rule when differentiating the log-determinant line restriction.
First derivatives of log det along positive-definite matrix segments in the concavity lemma and both directions of D-equivalence.
Computing g''(t)=−tr(Aₜ⁻¹HAₜ⁻¹H) in the log-determinant concavity proof.
Differentiating the trace in the log-determinant second-derivative calculation.
Coordinate derivations of trace cyclicity, rank-one leverage traces, tr Iₚ=p, and the support-weighted leverage identity.

seams_checked.note: The central composite definition uses precisely the full coded run set {−1,+1}ᵏ supplied by def-two-level-full-factorial-design. The supplier and consumer preserve k≥1 and coded coordinates; the consumer makes no unsupported orthogonality, variance, or estimability inference.

The central composite definition uses the regular fractional run set with declared independent generators, signs, and resolution. The supplier definition and its justified-by alias theorem support that interface, including run count and signed defining relations. The consumer separately qualifies the standard resolution-V-or-higher construction and asserts no automatic estimability or rotatability.
